# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and confers a substantial risk of ischemic stroke, largely attributable to thromboembolism originating in the left atrial appendage (LAA) [1]. Autopsy and transesophageal echocardiographic studies have demonstrated that more than 90% of thrombi in non-valvular AF form within the LAA, providing the anatomical rationale for mechanical exclusion of this structure [2]. While oral anticoagulation (OAC) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention, a significant proportion of patients have contraindications or poor adherence owing to bleeding risk [3]. Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) has emerged as an alternative for selected patients [4].

## Devices and Procedural Considerations

Several dedicated devices have been developed for transcatheter LAAC. The WATCHMAN device (Boston Scientific) is the most extensively studied, with the WATCHMAN FLX representing a refined iteration with improved sealing and safety [5,6]. The Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and its successor, the Amplatzer Amulet (Abbott), employ a distinct lobe-and-disc design that allows closure of a wider range of appendage morphologies [7,8]. Procedures are typically performed under general anesthesia or conscious sedation with transesophageal echocardiographic or intracardiac echocardiographic guidance, following transseptal puncture [9]. Accurate preprocedural imaging—using cardiac computed tomography or transesophageal echocardiography—is essential for device sizing and appreciation of the highly variable LAA morphology, classified as "chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower" types [10].

## Evidence Base

The pivotal PROTECT AF trial randomized patients with non-valvular AF to WATCHMAN implantation versus warfarin and demonstrated non-inferiority for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death [11]. The subsequent PREVAIL trial confirmed procedural safety improvements, though it narrowly missed one efficacy endpoint [12]. Long-term follow-up of these trials, including a patient-level meta-analysis, showed comparable stroke prevention with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality favoring LAAC [13,14]. Registry data, including the EWOLUTION study, corroborated high implant success rates and low complication rates in real-world practice [15]. The PRAGUE-17 trial extended this evidence by comparing LAAC with direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) in high-risk patients, demonstrating non-inferiority over long-term follow-up [16,17].

For the Amulet device, the AMULET IDE trial randomized patients against the WATCHMAN and showed non-inferiority for safety and effectiveness, with higher rates of complete appendage closure [18]. National registry analyses have further characterized contemporary procedural outcomes and learning-curve effects across large patient populations [19].

## Post-Procedural Management and Complications

Antithrombotic management following LAAC remains an area of ongoing investigation. Initial regimens used warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, but contemporary protocols increasingly employ short-course DOAC therapy or dual antiplatelet therapy, particularly in patients with high bleeding risk [20,21]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) is a recognized complication occurring in approximately 3–4% of patients and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk [22]. Peri-device leak, detected on follow-up imaging, may also carry clinical significance, although the threshold for clinical relevance remains debated [23]. Procedural complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access complications, the rates of which have declined with operator experience and device refinement [24].

## Patient Selection and Guidelines

Current guidelines provide a class IIb recommendation for LAAC in patients with non-valvular AF who have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation [25,26]. The 2024 European and American guidelines reflect evolving evidence supporting its role in carefully selected high–bleeding-risk patients [27]. Multidisciplinary heart-team evaluation and shared decision-making are emphasized given the procedural risks and the absence of large randomized comparisons specifically in OAC-ineligible patients [28].

## Future Directions

Ongoing randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and CATALYST, are comparing LAAC directly with DOAC therapy in broader populations and may expand indications if non-inferiority or superiority is demonstrated [29]. Concomitant LAAC during structural or electrophysiological procedures, advances in imaging-guided device selection, and strategies to reduce DRT represent active research frontiers. As evidence matures, LAAC is likely to assume a more prominent role in personalized stroke prevention for AF [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC offers a mechanical alternative to lifelong anticoagulation for stroke prevention in AF. Robust randomized and registry data support its efficacy and safety relative to warfarin and, increasingly, DOACs. Refinements in devices, imaging, and antithrombotic protocols continue to improve outcomes, while ongoing trials will define its optimal place in the therapeutic armamentarium.
